authored_against: High School Chemistry, Grade 10. Keys state established science at this course level; they are not extracted from the source, which states a focus and generic objectives.

fixed_facts: A physical property can be measured without changing the substance's identity; a chemical property describes how it changes into a different substance.
relationships: Physical properties include colour, state, melting and boiling point, density, hardness, and solubility; chemical properties include flammability, reactivity with acid, and resistance to corrosion.
Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of sample and can therefore identify a substance; extensive properties such as mass and volume cannot.
Observing a chemical property necessarily changes the sample, which is why chemical tests are destructive.
accepted_alternative_framings: Intensive and extensive, or amount-independent and amount-dependent, are equivalent framings.
disqualifying_errors: Using mass or volume as an identifying property of a substance.
Claiming flammability can be assessed without any change occurring.
Claiming a change of state produces a chemically different substance.
topics.out_of_scope: Spectroscopic identification and thermodynamic property tables are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The number of significant figures reported must reflect the precision of the instrument used.
relationships: A measurement is recorded to the smallest division of the instrument plus one estimated digit.
Precision describes how closely repeated measurements agree; accuracy describes how close they are to the accepted value, and the two are independent.
Calculations cannot create precision: a result is reported to no more significant figures than the least precise input allows.
accepted_alternative_framings: Reporting a value with an explicit uncertainty, or with significant figures alone, are both acceptable provided the precision claimed is real.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting a calculated result to more significant figures than the measurements support.
Treating precision and accuracy as the same property.
Claiming a measurement is accurate because repeated trials agreed closely.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal error propagation and statistical uncertainty analysis are beyond this course.

relationships: Repeated trials estimate random uncertainty; they do not detect or remove systematic error.
A systematic error shifts every trial in the same direction, so tightly agreeing results can still all be wrong.
A reported result states the number of trials and the spread among them, or a reader cannot judge it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the two error types as random and systematic, or as scatter and bias, are equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming repeated trials eliminate systematic error.
Discarding an outlying trial without recording that it was discarded and why.
Reporting a mean with no indication of spread or number of trials.
topics.out_of_scope: Standard deviation, confidence intervals, and outlier tests are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Density is mass divided by volume, and it is an intensive property: it does not change with the size of the sample.
relationships: Density is a derived quantity, calculated from two measurements, so its uncertainty depends on both.
Because density is intensive, a small piece and a large piece of the same pure substance have the same density.
Density varies with temperature, because volume does, so a density value is quoted with the temperature it applies at.
accepted_alternative_framings: Any consistent unit set is acceptable, provided mass and volume units are stated.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a larger sample of the same substance has a greater density.
Confusing density with mass, or treating a heavier object as necessarily denser.
Reporting a density with no units, or with units that are not mass over volume.
topics.out_of_scope: Thermal expansion coefficients and buoyancy calculations are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Mixtures are separated by physical means that exploit differences in properties; the components of a compound are separated only by chemical change.
relationships: Filtration exploits particle size, distillation exploits boiling point, chromatography exploits differing affinity, and evaporation exploits volatility.
Because a mixture's components keep their own properties, separation does not change the substances involved.
The choice of technique follows from which property differs most between the components.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a compound can be separated into its elements by filtration or distillation.
Claiming a homogeneous mixture is a pure substance because it looks uniform.
Claiming dissolving destroys the solute.
topics.out_of_scope: Chromatographic theory, fractional distillation column design, and separation efficiency are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A safety data sheet states hazards, handling, storage, first aid, and disposal for a specific substance.
relationships: Hazard information is specific to the substance and to its concentration and form; a dilute solution and a concentrated one are not interchangeable.
Hazard pictograms and hazard statements identify the type of hazard; the handling instructions state what to do about it.
Reading hazard information happens before the substance is handled, not after something goes wrong.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a household or naturally occurring substance is safe by virtue of being household or natural.
Applying hazard information for a concentrated substance to a dilute one, or the reverse, without saying so.
Claiming personal protective equipment removes a hazard rather than reducing exposure to it.
topics.out_of_scope: Regulatory classification systems and industrial exposure limits are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The number of protons in the nucleus defines the element.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
relationships: An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons outside it; protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons uncharged.
Changing the neutron number gives a different isotope of the same element; changing the proton number gives a different element.
Nearly all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus, while nearly all of its volume is the region occupied by electrons.
accepted_alternative_framings: Isotope notation by mass number, or by name and mass number, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming isotopes of an element differ in proton number.
Claiming an atom's identity is set by its electron count.
Claiming the mass of an atom is distributed evenly through its volume.
topics.out_of_scope: Nuclear binding energy calculations and quantum mechanical atomic models are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels; they do not have arbitrary intermediate energies.
relationships: Electrons occupy energy levels around the nucleus, with lower levels filled before higher ones in the ground state.
An electron moves between levels only by absorbing or emitting exactly the energy difference between them, which is why atomic spectra consist of discrete lines.
The arrangement of electrons, particularly in the outermost level, determines how an atom bonds.
accepted_alternative_framings: Shell diagrams, electron configuration notation, and orbital descriptions are all acceptable representations at this level.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed planetary paths at any energy.
Claiming an electron can absorb any amount of energy to move between levels.
Claiming inner electrons determine an atom's ordinary chemical bonding.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantum numbers, orbital shapes in detail, and spectroscopic term symbols are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost energy level, and they are the electrons involved in bonding.
relationships: The number of valence electrons largely determines an element's chemical behaviour, which is why elements in the same main group behave similarly.
Atoms tend toward outer-electron arrangements resembling those of the noble gases, by transferring, sharing, or delocalising electrons.
For main-group elements the valence electron count follows from the group: groups 1 and 2 have one and two, and groups 13 to 18 have the group number minus ten, with helium the exception at two.
accepted_alternative_framings: The octet rule and the noble-gas configuration description are equivalent framings; both have known exceptions.
disqualifying_errors: Counting all of an atom's electrons as valence electrons.
Claiming the octet rule holds without exception.
Claiming atoms bond in order to satisfy a preference or a need of their own.
topics.out_of_scope: Transition metal electron configurations and hypervalency are beyond this course.

topics.focus: periodic trends in atomic radius and ionization
fixed_facts: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group.
First ionisation energy generally increases across a period from left to right and decreases down a group.
relationships: Across a period, nuclear charge rises while electrons are added to the same energy level, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly.
Down a group, outer electrons occupy higher energy levels and are shielded by more inner electrons, so they are held less tightly.
The trends in radius and ionisation energy run in opposite directions because both follow from the same effective nuclear attraction.
accepted_alternative_framings: Explaining the trends through effective nuclear charge, or through nuclear charge together with shielding and energy level, are equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming atomic radius increases across a period from left to right.
Claiming ionisation energy increases down a group.
Claiming atoms get larger across a period because more electrons are added.
topics.out_of_scope: Slater's rules, quantitative effective nuclear charge, and irregularities in specific trends are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Reactivity increases down group 1 and decreases down group 17.
Noble gases are very unreactive because their outer energy level is already full.
relationships: Group 1 metals lose their single valence electron more readily further down the group, because that electron is held less tightly, so reactivity increases downward.
Group 17 elements gain an electron less readily further down the group, for the same reason, so reactivity decreases downward.
Similar valence electron arrangements are what make the elements of a group behave similarly.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the groups alkali metals, halogens, and noble gases, or by number, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming group 1 reactivity decreases down the group.
Claiming halogen reactivity increases down the group.
Claiming noble gases are unreactive because they have no electrons available.
topics.out_of_scope: Standard electrode potentials and transition metal reactivity series are beyond this course.

topics.focus: the periodic table as a predictive model
fixed_facts: The periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number, and elements with similar properties fall in the same group.
relationships: Because properties repeat with atomic number, the table predicts the behaviour of an element from its position.
The table's predictive power was demonstrated historically by successful predictions about elements not yet discovered.
The table is a model built on periodicity, and its predictions are approximate, with known exceptions.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the table is ordered by atomic mass rather than atomic number.
Claiming the table's predictions hold exactly with no exceptions.
Claiming position in the table causes an element's properties rather than reflecting its electron arrangement.
topics.out_of_scope: Relativistic effects on heavy element properties and superheavy element chemistry are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
Metallic bonding involves positive metal ions in a shared, delocalised sea of electrons.
relationships: Ionic bonds typically form between a metal and a non-metal, where the difference in attraction for electrons is large enough for transfer.
Covalent bonds typically form between non-metals, and the sharing is equal only when the two atoms attract electrons equally; otherwise the bond is polar.
Metallic bonding leaves electrons free to move through the structure, which is what makes metals conduct and deform without shattering.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing bond character as a continuum from pure covalent through polar covalent to ionic is more accurate than three discrete boxes, and is fully acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming ionic bonds form when atoms share electrons, equally or otherwise.
Claiming covalent bonds form by the transfer of electrons.
Claiming all covalent bonds share electrons equally, or that polar covalent bonds are ionic.
topics.out_of_scope: Molecular orbital theory, formal electronegativity cutoffs, and band theory are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules and are much weaker than the covalent bonds within a molecule.
relationships: Intermolecular attractions include dispersion forces, which act between all molecules, dipole-dipole attractions between polar molecules, and hydrogen bonding where hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
Boiling a molecular substance overcomes the forces between molecules, not the bonds within them.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling point, raise viscosity, and lower vapour pressure.
accepted_alternative_framings: London dispersion, van der Waals, and induced-dipole forces are acceptable names for the same interaction at this level.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming boiling water breaks the covalent bonds within water molecules.
Claiming hydrogen bonds are covalent bonds involving hydrogen.
Claiming non-polar molecules experience no intermolecular attraction at all.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative interaction energies and polarisability calculations are beyond this course.

topics.focus: bulk properties as evidence of particle forces
relationships: Bulk properties such as melting point, hardness, and volatility are evidence about the type and strength of the forces between particles.
Substances with strong three-dimensional networks of bonds, whether ionic or covalent network, have high melting points; molecular substances generally have low ones.
Reasoning runs from measured bulk property to inferred particle-level structure, and the inference is checked against other properties.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring bonding type from a single bulk property and stating it as established.
Claiming a high melting point on its own establishes ionic bonding, when covalent network solids also have high melting points.
Attributing a bulk property such as ductility to an individual particle.
topics.out_of_scope: Crystallography and lattice energy calculations are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Ionic compounds do not conduct as solids but do when molten or dissolved, because the ions become free to move.
Metals conduct in the solid state because their electrons are delocalised.
relationships: Electrical conduction requires charged particles free to move: delocalised electrons in metals, mobile ions in molten or dissolved ionic compounds.
Melting point reflects the energy needed to overcome the forces holding particles in the solid structure.
Solubility reflects whether the attractions formed with the solvent compensate for the attractions broken in the solute and the solvent.
accepted_alternative_framings: The heuristic that like dissolves like is acceptable, provided it is explained in terms of the attractions involved.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
Claiming a substance that dissolves must therefore conduct.
Claiming molecular covalent substances conduct because they contain electrons.
topics.out_of_scope: Conductivity measurement theory, solubility product constants, and lattice enthalpy cycles are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A polymer is a large molecule built from many repeating monomer units joined by covalent bonds.
relationships: A polymer's bulk properties follow from its monomer, its chain length, its branching, and the forces between chains.
Cross-linking between chains increases rigidity and reduces the ability to melt and flow.
Materials are designed by choosing structure to obtain properties, which is why structure-property reasoning is the core of materials design.
accepted_alternative_framings: Addition and condensation polymerisation are both correct classifications where the lesson calls for them.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a polymer is a mixture of its monomers rather than a molecule built from them.
Claiming a polymer's properties depend only on which monomer it is made from.
Claiming synthetic materials are not chemically related to the natural resources they are made from.
topics.out_of_scope: Polymerisation kinetics, molecular weight distributions, and copolymer theory are beyond this course.

relationships: A technical explanation states the claim, the evidence, and the particle-level reasoning that connects them.
Chemical notation, diagrams, and prose each carry different information, and the choice is made for what needs to be shown.
An explanation states the limits of the evidence rather than presenting an inference as a measurement.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting an inferred structure as though it had been directly observed.
Using chemical notation that does not match the substance being described.
Stating a conclusion with more certainty than the evidence supports.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal technical writing standards and publication conventions are beyond this course.

relationships: A chemical change produces substances with different properties from the starting materials.
Indicators include gas evolution, unexplained temperature change, colour change, precipitate formation, light emission, and odour, each of which has non-chemical explanations too.
The strongest evidence is a measured change in an identifying property before and after.
disqualifying_errors: Treating bubbling alone as proof of reaction, when boiling and dissolved gas release also produce bubbles.
Claiming dissolving is a chemical change.
Concluding a reaction occurred from one ambiguous observation with no control.
topics.out_of_scope: Instrumental analysis and reaction monitoring techniques are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Common reaction patterns include synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion.
relationships: Classifying a reaction by pattern supports predicting its products, because each pattern has a characteristic rearrangement.
The classification describes what happens to the atoms, not why the reaction is favourable.
Some reactions fit more than one pattern, and some fit none; the categories are a useful model rather than an exhaustive partition.
accepted_alternative_framings: Combination and synthesis are the same category; single and double displacement and replacement are the same categories.
disqualifying_errors: Predicting products by pattern while producing an equation in which atoms are not conserved.
Claiming classification by pattern establishes that a reaction will occur.
Claiming every reaction fits exactly one of the standard categories.
topics.out_of_scope: Reaction mechanisms, activity series in quantitative form, and organic reaction classification are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Chemical reactions involve rearrangement of outer electrons; nuclei are unchanged.
relationships: In a chemical reaction, valence electrons are transferred, shared, or redistributed, and the nuclei retain their identity.
This is why elements are conserved in chemical reactions: no atom becomes an atom of a different element.
The stability of the resulting outer-electron arrangements is part of why some rearrangements are favourable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming atoms of one element are converted into another element by a chemical reaction.
Claiming nuclear particles are rearranged during ordinary chemical reactions.
Claiming inner-shell electrons participate in ordinary chemical bonding.
topics.out_of_scope: Nuclear reactions belong to unit 9; orbital hybridisation is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together: electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
relationships: In a redox reaction, the species oxidised is the reducing agent and the species reduced is the oxidising agent.
Because electrons are conserved, the electrons lost in the oxidation equal the electrons gained in the reduction.
Combustion, corrosion, and electrochemical cells are all redox processes.
accepted_alternative_framings: The mnemonics for loss and gain of electrons, and descriptions in terms of oxidation number changes, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming oxidation is gain of electrons or reduction is loss of electrons.
Claiming oxidation can occur without a corresponding reduction.
Claiming oxidation requires the presence of oxygen.
topics.out_of_scope: Standard electrode potentials, Nernst equation, and balancing redox in acidic or basic solution are beyond this course.

relationships: Position in the periodic table indicates likely charges for main-group ions, and therefore likely formulas for the compounds formed.
A predicted product is a hypothesis to be checked against conservation of atoms, charge balance, and experimental evidence.
Trends give likely outcomes, not guarantees; exceptions exist and are part of the chemistry.
disqualifying_errors: Predicting a compound whose formula does not balance charge.
Presenting a trend-based prediction as an established result with no verification.
Claiming a reaction must occur because the products would be reasonable.
topics.out_of_scope: Thermodynamic prediction of spontaneity and quantitative equilibrium prediction are beyond this course.

relationships: A chemical explanation connects observation to particle-level behaviour by explicit reasoning.
Revising an explanation means saying what evidence prompted the change and what the earlier version got wrong.
An explanation that accounts for the confirming evidence but not the disconfirming evidence is incomplete.
disqualifying_errors: Revising an explanation to fit new evidence without saying what the earlier version failed to account for.
Presenting an explanation that ignores an observation that contradicts it.
Describing what was observed and calling it an explanation.
topics.out_of_scope: Philosophy of scientific explanation and formal model selection are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The number of atoms of each element is identical before and after a chemical reaction, so mass is conserved.
relationships: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions; they are rearranged among substances.
Conservation of atoms is the reason chemical equations must balance and the reason mass calculations work.
An apparent mass change in an open system means matter crossed the system boundary, most often as a gas.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is lost during combustion without accounting for oxygen consumed and gases released.
Claiming atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Concluding that mass is not conserved from an open-container measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Mass-energy equivalence, which does apply to nuclear reactions, is unit 9 work.

fixed_facts: Balancing an equation is done by changing coefficients only; subscripts in a formula are never changed to make an equation balance.
relationships: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the same total charge.
Coefficients represent relative numbers of particles or moles, and they scale the whole formula unit they precede.
Changing a subscript changes the substance, which is why balancing never alters subscripts.
accepted_alternative_framings: Any set of coefficients in the correct ratio balances the equation; the lowest whole-number set is conventional but not the only correct answer.
disqualifying_errors: Altering a subscript in a chemical formula in order to balance an equation.
Presenting an equation as balanced when the atom counts differ between sides.
Claiming coefficients represent masses rather than numbers of particles or moles.
topics.out_of_scope: Balancing redox half-reactions in solution and matrix methods are beyond this course.

topics.focus: the mole as a counting unit
fixed_facts: One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, approximately 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third.
relationships: The mole is a counting unit for particles, in the same way that a dozen is, chosen so that molar mass in grams matches atomic and formula mass.
A mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, but moles of different substances have different masses.
The particle counted must be specified, since a mole of oxygen atoms and a mole of oxygen molecules are different quantities.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a mole is a unit of mass.
Claiming a mole of every substance has the same mass.
Using a mole quantity without specifying whether atoms, molecules, or formula units are counted.
topics.out_of_scope: The current SI definition of the mole in terms of a fixed Avogadro constant is acceptable to state but not required.

fixed_facts: The molar mass of a substance in grams per mole is numerically equal to its formula or molecular mass in atomic mass units.
relationships: Molar mass is calculated by summing the molar masses of the atoms in the formula, each multiplied by its subscript.
Molar mass converts between mass, which is measurable, and moles, which is what stoichiometry needs.
The molar mass of an element as listed on the periodic table is a weighted average across its natural isotopes.
disqualifying_errors: Summing atomic masses without applying the subscripts in the formula.
Claiming the periodic table mass is the mass of a single specified isotope.
Reporting a molar mass without units, or with units other than mass per mole.
topics.out_of_scope: Mass spectrometry and precise isotopic abundance determination are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and therefore determines how much product can form.
relationships: The limiting reactant is identified by comparing available amounts in moles against the ratio the balanced equation requires, not by comparing masses.
Reactant left over when the reaction stops is in excess, and it does not increase the yield.
Theoretical yield follows from the limiting reactant; actual yield is measured and is normally lower.
disqualifying_errors: Identifying the limiting reactant as the one present in the smallest mass without converting to moles.
Claiming adding more of the excess reactant increases the product yield.
Calculating theoretical yield from the excess reactant.
topics.out_of_scope: Percent yield error analysis and multi-step yield propagation are acceptable but not required.

relationships: A balanced equation is a mathematical statement about relative numbers of particles, and mole ratios are read directly from its coefficients.
Mass, moles, and particle count are related through molar mass and Avogadro's number, and calculations move between them in a stated order.
A calculated result carries the units and the precision of the measurements it came from.
accepted_alternative_framings: Dimensional analysis and proportional reasoning both yield correct results and are equally acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Reading mole ratios from an unbalanced equation.
Applying coefficients as mass ratios rather than mole ratios.
Reporting a calculated result with more significant figures than the input measurements support.
topics.out_of_scope: Solution stoichiometry with concentration and gas law stoichiometry are acceptable but not required here.

fixed_facts: Breaking a chemical bond requires an input of energy; forming a chemical bond releases energy.
relationships: Energy must be supplied to separate bonded atoms, because the bond exists precisely because the bonded state is lower in energy.
Energy is released when atoms come together to form a bond.
The overall energy change of a reaction is the difference between the energy required to break bonds and the energy released in forming them.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming breaking bonds releases energy.
Claiming forming bonds requires a net energy input.
Claiming a molecule such as ATP or glucose releases energy by having its bonds broken alone, with no account of the bonds formed.
topics.out_of_scope: Bond enthalpy tables and quantitative enthalpy calculations are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: An exothermic process releases energy to the surroundings; an endothermic process absorbs energy from them.
relationships: In an exothermic reaction the products are lower in chemical energy than the reactants, and the difference is released to the surroundings.
In an endothermic reaction the products are higher in chemical energy, and the difference is absorbed from the surroundings.
The surroundings warming or cooling is the evidence; the reaction system itself is what is being classified.
accepted_alternative_framings: Energy diagrams, enthalpy sign conventions, and plain descriptions of energy released or absorbed are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an endothermic reaction produces cold rather than absorbing energy.
Claiming an exothermic reaction creates energy.
Confusing the reaction being exothermic with the reaction being fast or spontaneous.
topics.out_of_scope: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity criteria are beyond this course.

relationships: The net energy change is the total energy needed to break all bonds in the reactants minus the total released in forming all bonds in the products.
If more energy is released in forming bonds than was required to break them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise it is endothermic.
Bond energy values are averages across compounds, so calculations from them give estimates rather than exact results.
disqualifying_errors: Computing an energy change from bond breaking alone, ignoring bond formation.
Reversing the sign convention so that bond breaking is treated as releasing energy.
Presenting an estimate from average bond energies as an exact measured value.
topics.out_of_scope: Hess's law cycles and calorimetric enthalpy determination are acceptable but not required.

fixed_facts: Thermal energy transfers spontaneously from the higher-temperature body to the lower-temperature one until they reach the same temperature.
relationships: Two bodies in thermal contact exchange energy until their temperatures are equal, which is thermal equilibrium.
Temperature is a measure of average particle kinetic energy; total thermal energy also depends on the amount and the material.
The energy lost by one body equals the energy gained by the other and its surroundings; energy is conserved.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming cold flows from the cooler body into the warmer one.
Treating temperature and total thermal energy as the same quantity.
Claiming thermal energy moves spontaneously from a cooler body to a warmer one.
topics.out_of_scope: Specific heat calculations are acceptable but not required; entropy is treated qualitatively in this unit.

relationships: A computational energy model represents the system's energy inputs, outputs, and stores, and it must balance.
The model's output depends on the assumptions and parameters entered, and both are stated with the result.
A model result is a prediction, and it is compared against measurement rather than substituted for it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Spreadsheet, diagram, and equation-based models are all acceptable forms here.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting model output as though it were experimental data.
Building an energy model whose inputs and outputs do not balance.
Reporting a model result without stating its assumptions.
topics.out_of_scope: Numerical methods and molecular simulation are beyond this course.

topics.focus: the second law in everyday systems
fixed_facts: Energy spontaneously disperses; concentrating it in a system requires energy input from elsewhere.
relationships: Energy is conserved in every process, but its usefulness decreases as it disperses into the surroundings.
A refrigerator or heat pump moves thermal energy from cooler to warmer only because work is done on it, so the overall dispersal still increases.
This is why no device converts all energy input into useful output, and why perpetual motion machines are impossible.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the principle through entropy, through energy dispersal, or through the impossibility of a perfect engine are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a device can be one hundred per cent efficient in converting energy to useful work.
Claiming the second law is violated by any local decrease in disorder, without accounting for the surroundings.
Confusing conservation of energy with conservation of useful energy.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative entropy calculation and statistical thermodynamics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with sufficient energy and in a suitable orientation.
relationships: Reaction rate depends on how often effective collisions occur, where effective means both energetic enough and correctly oriented.
Activation energy is the minimum energy a collision must have to lead to reaction.
Anything that raises the frequency or the effectiveness of collisions raises the rate.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every collision between reactant particles produces a reaction.
Claiming orientation is irrelevant provided the collision is energetic enough.
Confusing activation energy with the overall energy change of the reaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Rate laws, rate constants, and the Arrhenius equation are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Raising the temperature increases reaction rate.
relationships: Higher temperature increases the average kinetic energy of particles, so collisions are both more frequent and more often energetic enough to react.
The increase in the fraction of sufficiently energetic collisions is the larger of the two effects.
Temperature affects rate; it does not change whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming higher temperature works only by making collisions more frequent.
Claiming raising the temperature changes a reaction from endothermic to exothermic.
Claiming temperature has no effect on the rate of an exothermic reaction.
topics.out_of_scope: Arrhenius plots and quantitative temperature coefficients are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Increasing the concentration of a reactant generally increases the reaction rate.
relationships: Higher concentration means more reactant particles in a given volume, so collisions between them are more frequent.
Concentration affects collision frequency but not the energy of individual collisions.
For gases, increasing pressure by reducing volume has the same effect as increasing concentration.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming higher concentration increases the energy of each collision.
Claiming concentration changes the activation energy.
Claiming rate depends on the total amount of reactant rather than on its concentration.
topics.out_of_scope: Reaction order and rate law determination are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant increases the reaction rate.
relationships: A reaction involving a solid occurs at its surface, so subdividing the solid exposes more particles to collision.
Mixing brings reactants into contact and prevents local depletion, which is why stirring can raise the rate in solution.
Surface area and mixing affect how often reactant particles meet, not the energy of the collisions.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the mass of a solid, rather than its exposed surface area, sets the rate for a surface reaction.
Claiming subdividing a solid changes its chemical properties.
Claiming stirring changes the activation energy.
topics.out_of_scope: Diffusion-limited kinetics and surface chemistry are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing a pathway with lower activation energy, and it is not consumed by the reaction.
relationships: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is effective at any given temperature.
A catalyst does not change the overall energy change of the reaction or the position of equilibrium; it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally.
Enzymes are biological catalysts and follow the same principles.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a catalyst is consumed by the reaction it catalyses.
Claiming a catalyst increases the yield or shifts the equilibrium position.
Claiming a catalyst supplies the activation energy rather than lowering it.
topics.out_of_scope: Catalytic mechanisms, turnover number, and heterogeneous catalysis theory are beyond this course.

relationships: A rate explanation identifies which factor was changed and connects it to collision frequency, collision energy, or activation energy.
Naming the factor is description; connecting it to the collision model is explanation.
An explanation is tested by whether it also predicts what happens when the factor is changed the other way.
disqualifying_errors: Attributing a rate change to a factor without identifying the mechanism it acts through.
Attributing a rate increase to lowered activation energy when the factor changed was temperature or concentration.
Claiming a factor speeds a reaction because it makes the reaction more favourable energetically.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative kinetics and mechanism determination are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions, and reactants are never completely converted to products in a closed system.
relationships: In a reversible reaction the products re-form the reactants as well as the reverse, so both are present at all times.
The double arrow notation states that both directions occur under the same conditions.
Reversibility is a property of the reaction under the stated conditions, not a claim that it can be undone by any means.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a reversible reaction goes to completion in a closed system.
Claiming the reverse reaction begins only after the forward reaction has finished.
Claiming reversibility means the reaction produces no net change ever.
topics.out_of_scope: Equilibrium constant expressions and quantitative equilibrium calculation are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so concentrations remain constant while both reactions continue.
relationships: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates, and the system is not static.
Equal rates do not mean equal concentrations; the concentrations at equilibrium depend on the reaction.
Equilibrium is reached only in a closed system, since an open one loses products or reactants.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming reactions stop at equilibrium.
Claiming equilibrium means equal concentrations of reactants and products.
Claiming an open system with material escaping can reach equilibrium.
topics.out_of_scope: Equilibrium constants, reaction quotients, and equilibrium calculations are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A system at equilibrium responds to a change in conditions by shifting in the direction that partially counteracts that change.
relationships: Changing concentration, pressure, or temperature disturbs the balance of forward and reverse rates, and the system shifts until they are equal again.
The shift partially offsets the change; it does not restore the original conditions.
Temperature is the only one of these changes that alters the equilibrium position by changing the balance of the reaction's own energetics rather than by changing amounts.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming this Le Chatelier's principle, or describing the response without the name, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the system returns exactly to its original conditions after a disturbance.
Claiming a catalyst shifts the position of equilibrium.
Claiming adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts a gas-phase equilibrium.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative prediction of the new equilibrium position is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward products; increasing pressure on a gas-phase equilibrium shifts it toward the side with fewer gas particles.
relationships: Adding a substance shifts the system away from that substance; removing one shifts it toward that substance.
For gas-phase equilibria, raising pressure by reducing volume favours the side with fewer moles of gas.
Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction; lowering it favours the exothermic direction.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming raising temperature always increases product yield regardless of the reaction's energetics.
Claiming pressure changes shift an equilibrium with equal moles of gas on both sides.
Claiming a catalyst changes the yield at equilibrium.
topics.out_of_scope: Van't Hoff analysis and quantitative yield prediction are beyond this course.

relationships: Industrial conditions balance equilibrium yield against reaction rate, energy cost, equipment limits, and safety.
Conditions that maximise yield often reduce rate, and the chosen compromise is not the maximum of either.
Recycling unreacted material raises overall conversion without changing the equilibrium position.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming industrial conditions are chosen to maximise equilibrium yield alone.
Claiming a catalyst is used to increase the yield rather than the rate.
Presenting a set of conditions as optimal with no criteria or constraints stated.
topics.out_of_scope: Process engineering economics and reactor design are beyond this course.

relationships: Refining a chemical system means changing one condition at a time and measuring the effect against stated criteria.
A change that improves one criterion commonly worsens another, and the trade-off is reported.
Safety and waste constraints bound the design space and are not traded for yield or rate.
disqualifying_errors: Changing several conditions at once and attributing the improvement to one.
Reporting a design as improved without measuring against the stated criteria.
Trading a safety or waste constraint for better yield.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal process optimisation and life-cycle assessment are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The atomic number is the number of protons and identifies the element; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.
relationships: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and differ in neutron number, and therefore in mass number.
Isotopes of an element have essentially identical chemical behaviour, because chemistry depends on electrons, while their nuclear stability can differ greatly.
The mass listed on the periodic table is a weighted average over an element's naturally occurring isotopes.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming isotopes of an element differ chemically in a substantial way.
Claiming the mass number is the mass in grams.
Claiming an element's isotopes have different proton numbers.
topics.out_of_scope: Nuclear shell models and binding energy per nucleon curves are acceptable to reference but not required.

fixed_facts: Half-life is the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay, and it is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical combination.
Alpha decay reduces the atomic number by two and the mass number by four; beta-minus decay increases the atomic number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged.
relationships: Radioactive decay is a nuclear process, so it changes the element, unlike chemical reactions.
Decay of an individual nucleus is random, while the behaviour of a large sample follows a predictable exponential pattern.
Half-life is a constant for a given nuclide and does not depend on how much of the sample remains.
accepted_alternative_framings: Decay described by half-life, or by fraction remaining after a number of half-lives, are equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming half-life can be changed by heating, cooling, or chemically combining the substance.
Claiming a sample is completely gone after two half-lives.
Claiming radioactive decay is a chemical reaction involving electrons.
topics.out_of_scope: Decay constants, activity units, and dosimetry are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and typically neutrons.
relationships: Fission of a heavy nucleus releases energy because the products are more tightly bound per nucleon than the original nucleus.
Released neutrons can induce further fissions, which is the basis of a chain reaction.
Control of a fission reactor works by controlling the number of neutrons available to induce further fission.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming fission is the combining of nuclei.
Claiming fission energy comes from breaking chemical bonds.
Claiming a reactor's fuel can undergo a nuclear explosion in the manner of a weapon.
topics.out_of_scope: Reactor engineering, cross sections, and criticality calculations are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Fusion is the combining of light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
Fusion powers the Sun and other stars.
relationships: Fusion releases energy because the product nucleus is more tightly bound per nucleon than the light nuclei that formed it.
Fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure, because positively charged nuclei repel each other strongly at short range.
That requirement is why sustained controlled fusion for power generation remains an engineering problem.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming fusion is the splitting of nuclei.
Claiming fusion occurs readily at ordinary temperatures.
Claiming the Sun is powered by chemical combustion.
topics.out_of_scope: Plasma physics and confinement approaches are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In nuclear reactions a small amount of mass is converted to energy, following the mass-energy relationship, which is why nuclear energy release is millions of times larger per event than chemical energy release.
relationships: The energy released in a nuclear reaction corresponds to the mass difference between the initial and final nuclei.
Chemical reactions rearrange electrons and involve mass changes far too small to measure; nuclear reactions do not.
This difference in scale is why a small mass of nuclear fuel yields energy comparable to a very large mass of chemical fuel.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is conserved exactly in nuclear reactions in the same way it is in chemical ones.
Claiming chemical and nuclear energy releases are of comparable magnitude per reaction.
Claiming nuclear energy comes from breaking bonds between atoms.
topics.out_of_scope: Relativistic mechanics and binding energy computation are beyond this course.

topics.focus: criteria, constraints, and trade-offs in chemical engineering
relationships: A chemical engineering design is evaluated against stated criteria such as yield, rate, cost, and energy demand, within constraints of safety, waste, and regulation.
Improving one criterion usually costs something on another, and the design states which trade-off was accepted and why.
Waste streams and end-of-life handling are part of the design, not a consequence to be addressed afterwards.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a design as optimal on every criterion simultaneously.
Omitting waste or safety from the evaluation.
Declaring a design successful with no criteria stated to judge it against.
topics.out_of_scope: Process economics, regulatory compliance procedure, and formal life-cycle assessment are beyond this course.
